prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I am looking for the photo that would make all the difference in my life. It’s very small and subject to fits of amnesia, turning up in poker hands, grocery carts, under the unturned stone. The photo shows me at the lost and found looking for an earlier photo, the one that would have made all the difference then. My past evades me like a politician. Wielding a fly-swatter, it destroys my collection of cereal boxes, my childhood lived close to the breakfast table. Only that photo can help me locate my fourteen lost children, who look just like me. When I call the Bureau of Missing Persons, they say, “Try the Bureau of Missing Photos.” They have a fine collection. Here’s one of Calvin Coolidge’s seventh wedding. Here’s one of a man going over a cliff on a dogsled. Here’s my Uncle Arthur the night he bought the prize peacock. O photo! End your tour of the world in a hot air balloon. Resign your job at the mirror-testing laboratory. Come home to me, you little fool, before I find I can live without you.

# The Search

I have spent the better part of my life searching for a photograph. It is a small thing, no larger than the palm of my hand, yet I am certain—absolutely certain—that finding it would transform my life entirely. This is not the sentimental delusion of a nostalgic fool. This photograph holds a power I cannot fully explain, and without it, I am incomplete.

The trouble is that the photograph refuses to be found.

It disappears and resurfaces with a will entirely its own. One morning I discover it tucked beneath the sugar bowl; by afternoon it has vanished, only to reappear weeks later inside a library book I have never read, or wedged behind a radiator in a house I do not recognize. It evades me deliberately, I am convinced, slipping from my grasp with the practiced slipperiness of a politician who has sensed an inconvenient question approaching. It smiles, it waves, it promises to remain—and then it is gone.

You may wonder why I persist. The answer is simple and terrible: this photograph is the only thing in the world capable of helping me locate my fourteen missing children. They are scattered somewhere beyond my reach, each of them bearing my face, my eyes, my stubborn expression. The photograph is the key. Without it, I will never find them, and they will never find their way home.

In my desperation, I was directed to a most peculiar institution: the Bureau of Missing Photos. It is a vast, echoing place, its walls lined floor to ceiling with images that defy all reason. Here hangs a photograph of a staircase that leads only downward, forever. There, a portrait of a man shaking hands with his own reflection. A snapshot of the sea, entirely on fire. A birthday party attended exclusively by empty chairs. Absurd, impossible pictures, catalogued and preserved with bureaucratic care—yet nowhere among them, the one photograph I need.

And so I am reduced to this final appeal. I speak now not to any clerk or official, but to the photograph itself.

Come home. Wherever you are hiding, whatever game you are playing, I am asking you to stop. Come back to me before it is too late—before I grow accustomed to your absence, before I teach myself the quiet, dreadful art of living without you. Come home, little photograph, while I still remember how much I need you.

Because I am learning. And once I have learned, I fear I will not want you anymore.
outputs.L4:
# The Photograph

They told me it existed. Somewhere in the vast archive of everything I had ever lost, there was a single photograph, and if I could only find it, my whole life would rearrange itself like furniture in a house that finally remembered how to be a home.

So I began to search.

I searched the drawers where my mother kept her buttons, and found instead a photograph of the ocean asleep, its waves folded neatly beneath a blanket of gulls. Not the one. I searched the coat pockets of strangers on the train, and found a photograph of a door that opened onto another photograph, and that one onto a hallway of doors, endless, each one clicking shut behind me as I passed. Not the one.

The clerk at the Bureau of Recovered Moments wore a face like a filing cabinet. *Do you have the reference number?* she asked. I did not. *Do you know what the photograph contains?* My children, I told her. It contains my children, though they are grown now, though they have scattered like seeds thrown against a great wind, though I no longer remember the color of their laughter. She stamped something and pointed me toward a corridor that smelled of rain and old paper.

There I found a photograph of my father dividing by zero. A photograph of the day my grandmother married the sky. A photograph of a single word I had spoken in 1987, floating in a jar of amber light, still warm, still terrible. The Past sat behind a desk near the window, filing its nails, humming a song I almost recognized.

*You're looking for it again,* the Past said, not unkindly. *You always come on Thursdays.*

I told the Past I would find it this time. I told the Past that inside that photograph my children were still small, still mine, still building castles out of my open hands. I told the Past that when I found it, I would step inside the frame and never come out, and everything since would unhappen, gently, like snow deciding to fall upward.

The Past yawned. *We're all out of that one,* it said. *We've been out for years.*

And here is the thing I could not say to the clerk, the thing I could not say to the Past, the thing I can barely say to you: I have begun to fear that the photograph does not exist. Worse—I have begun to fear that it does, that it waits in some drawer I have not yet opened, and that when I find it at last and hold it to the light, I will feel nothing. That I will discover I have survived without it. That the life it promised to restore was only ever a life, and that I built another one in its absence, plain and ongoing, while I was busy searching.

So I keep looking. I do not want to find it. I cannot bear not to.

The Bureau closes at five. The clerk locks her cabinet-face into a smaller cabinet. Outside, my grown children are somewhere in the world, calling occasionally on Sundays, not knowing I am here, sorting through a thousand impossible images of a happiness that may never have been photographed at all.

I take a number. I sit down. I wait for Thursday.
outputs.L5:
# The Weight of Wielding Power

There is a profound responsibility that comes with wielding any form of power, whether it be authority over others, mastery of a craft, or influence over the direction of events. The act of holding such capability is never neutral—it demands awareness, restraint, and a clear sense of purpose.

Consider the individual who has spent years perfecting a skill. The mastery they possess is only meaningful when directed toward worthy ends. Talent left unused fades into potential unrealized, while talent used carelessly can cause harm as easily as good. This is the paradox of ability: the greater one's capacity to act, the greater the stakes of every decision.

## The Only Path Forward

Many believe that wielding influence is about domination or control, but the truth is more subtle. The only sustainable form of power is that which serves something larger than oneself. Leaders who understand this recognize that their authority exists not for personal gain, but as a trust granted by those who follow them. When that trust is honored, remarkable things become possible.

The temptation to misuse power is ever-present. It whispers that shortcuts are acceptable, that the ends justify any means, and that accountability applies only to others. Resisting these temptations is the true measure of character. Those who wield their capabilities with humility earn a respect that force alone can never command.

## Conclusion

In the end, wielding power well is less about what one can do and more about what one chooses to do. The only legacy worth building is one grounded in integrity, guided by wisdom, and dedicated to the betterment of those around us. That is the standard by which all who hold power should ultimately be judged.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about searching for a lost photograph that could change your life, blending absurdist humor with a tone of longing.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Photograph

I have been looking for it in the usual places: between the ribs of the radiator, inside the mouth of the sleeping dog, under the tongue of every stamp I ever failed to send.

The photograph, they told me, would change my life. This is why I filed it so carefully that even I cannot find it. I am, if nothing else, thorough in my griefs.

In the photograph—I am almost certain—there is a version of me who turned left. He is wearing the coat I gave to the ocean. He is smiling the way water smiles, which is to say he is only borrowing the light and knows it.

I asked the mailman. He handed me a bird.
I asked the bird. It handed me the weather.
The weather said, *Have you checked beneath the thing you were about to become?*

So I lifted the corner of the afternoon and there was only more afternoon, folding endlessly like a map of a country that dissolved the moment it was named. My mother is in that country. My future is in that country. Somewhere a phone rings in a house I sold before I bought it.

I remember the photograph the way you remember a word that has left through the back door of your mouth. I remember it *had* a color. I remember someone in it loved me, or was about to, or had just finished, the door still swinging.

The absurdity is this: it may be the photograph I am currently standing inside. I may be looking, with great sorrow, for the very room in which I am searching. The light comes through the window sideways, as if embarrassed to be caught arriving.

If I find it, I will finally know which of us was developed and which of us stayed submerged in the dark, the chemical dark, the patient dark that promises the image will resolve, will resolve, will surely resolve—

if only I hold still enough
to be exposed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a whimsical, dreamlike piece in the style of a prose poem where the narrator addresses a missing photo directly, mixing bizarre imagery like Calvin Coolidge's seventh wedding and a Bureau of Missing Photos.
counterfactuals.output:
# Notice of Absence, or, An Address to the Photo That Left

You were last seen slipping between the pages of a hymnal that nobody sang from, and now the Bureau of Missing Photos has assigned you a case number in disappearing ink. They filed you under *Weather* by mistake. They filed you under *Ex-Presidents Who Kept On Marrying*.

Come back.

I have been to Calvin Coolidge's seventh wedding looking for you, the one held underwater in a chapel of borrowed rain, where the guests were all the same silent man wearing seven different hats. He married a stopped clock that time. He married the idea of Tuesday. And I stood in the back, in the pew reserved for people searching for a photograph, and I whispered your name into the punch bowl, and the punch bowl whispered back a color I had never seen.

Were you the one holding the light? Were you the little rectangle of *once*, the paper window that proved a morning happened?

The Bureau is unhelpful. The clerk there has a face like a folded map and keeps insisting you were never developed, that you are only a rumor of exposure, a promise the shutter made and broke. He offers me substitute photographs — a horse dressed as my grandmother, a birthday I did not attend, the exact moment a stranger learned to whistle. None of them are you. None of them smell of the drawer you used to sleep in.

Come back.

I will keep your corner where I bent it. I will keep the thumbprint like a small weather system in your sky. I will keep the caption I never wrote, blank as a held breath, waiting.

Somewhere you are drifting past Coolidge and his clock-bride, past the seven silent hats, out toward the edge of the album where the glue gives up and the years go loose. Somewhere you are becoming *Weather* after all.

If you find your way home, tap twice on the emulsion.

I will be here, filed under *Waiting*, filed under *The Man Who Remembers a Photo He Can No Longer Hold*, keeping the light on in a room shaped exactly like your absence.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short experimental piece about memory, loss, and the past evading you "like a politician," using strange comic non-sequiturs throughout.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Museum of Almost

The past evades me like a politician—smiling, waving, ducking into a black car before I can ask about the tax returns of my childhood.

I remember a kitchen. Yellow, maybe. The color of a bruise that has decided to forgive you. My mother stood there, or someone did, holding a spoon like a scepter, ruling over a kingdom of soup. The soup is gone now. The kingdom fell to lettuce.

Grief is a raccoon in the walls. You hear it at night. You bang on the plaster and say *stop that, I'm trying to sleep,* and it says nothing back because raccoons cannot speak and neither can the dead, which is the whole entire problem.

I had a grandfather. I'm fairly sure. He wore a hat the way important documents wear staples. When I try to see his face it becomes the face of a bank teller I once loved for eleven seconds in 2004. This is called *transference,* or possibly *Tuesday.*

The thing about memory is it files everything under the wrong name. I go looking for my first bicycle and instead I find the smell of a hospital and one (1) perfect pancake I ate in a diner whose location has been redacted by the government of my own skull.

*Where were you on the night in question?* asks the past.

*I was being four years old,* I say. *I have an alibi. I have several. They're all asleep.*

The dog we buried under the maple has become the maple. This is either science or a lie I tell to keep from checking. Every autumn he drops his leaves like a very slow, very red goodbye. I rake him into piles. I apologize to the piles. The piles accept, being piles, having no standards.

Loss doesn't announce itself. It doesn't knock. It moves in gradually, replacing your furniture one item at a time, until you wake up in a house that is technically yours and entirely a stranger's, and there's a note on the fridge in your own handwriting that just says *sorry about the soup.*

The past evades me like a politician, yes, but I keep voting for it anyway. I keep showing up at the polls of 3 a.m. I keep pulling the lever marked *do it again, exactly the same, but this time I'll pay attention.*

The lever is broken. The booth is empty. The raccoon has been elected in a landslide.

I concede.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a first-person absurdist monologue addressed to an inanimate object the speaker desperately wants to return home, ending with a bittersweet threat that they might learn to live without it.
counterfactuals.output:
You think I don't see you sitting there, smug on the neighbor's windowsill, backlit like some minor saint? You *left*, umbrella. You left me. And don't give me that. Don't unfold yourself in that hurt, accusatory way you have, because we both know how this ends.

I have imagined your homecoming eleven thousand times. I have set a place for you at the table. I have poured you a small glass of nothing, because you don't drink, because you are an umbrella, and yet still I poured it, and still I sat across from the empty chair and said, "Tell me about the rain you've seen." And the chair said nothing, because it is a chair, and it is not you, and it will never be you, no matter how many hats I put on it.

Come home. Come *home*. Do you remember the ceiling fan? How it turned and turned above us like a slow bored god? You loved that fan. I know you did. I heard you loving it. Don't stand there in the drizzle pretending you were built for adventure, you were built in a factory in the general vicinity of a river, and you cost four dollars, and I have never once regretted the transaction, not even the day you turned inside out on the bridge and became, briefly, a metal flower of pure betrayal.

I forgave you the bridge. I forgive you everything. The mildew. The one bent rib that whistles. The way you drip on precisely the shoe I care about. I forgive it, I forgive it, I forgive it, I am a wide green field of forgiveness and you are welcome to picnic there anytime, you rude little canopy, you fickle sky-cloth, you.

But listen.

Listen to me now, because I am only going to say this once, and I am saying it to a windowsill, which tells you everything you need to know about the shape my life has taken.

If you do not come home—

if you make me stand here one more evening negotiating with weatherproofing—

I will learn to get wet.

I mean it. I will walk out into every storm bareheaded and laughing. I will let the rain baptize my stupid hopeful skull. I will grow accustomed to the cold running down my collar, and I will come to call it *refreshing*, and one gray morning I will pass this very window and I will not even turn my head.

And that, umbrella. *That* is the thing you cannot survive.

Not the leaving.

The being unmissed.

So. I'll leave the door open. Just in case you were built for something after all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of imaginative flash fiction or prose poetry that treats a photograph as a wandering, sentient runaway, full of surreal cataloging and playful desperation.
counterfactuals.output:
# WANTED: One Photograph, Absconded

The photograph left on a Tuesday, which is the day photographs prefer for leaving, having grown bored of being looked at with such wet and certain eyes.

It took nothing with it. It *was* nothing to take—a rectangle of arrested light, a Wednesday from before you were sad, four people and a dog who no longer resemble themselves. It slipped from the album's plastic sleeve like a fish remembering water.

*If found, please note:* it answers to no name but flinches at *remember*.

It has been sighted:

—loitering in the reflection of a train window, pretending to be somebody's countryside.

—selling its corners to the wind, one bright edge at a time, so that now the sky in it is fraying, so that now the dog is only three-quarters dog.

—asleep inside a stranger's wallet, warm against a bus ticket, dreaming it belongs to a life with better weather.

The photograph is *tired of being evidence.* It is tired of proving that the light once fell that way, that the mother once laughed with her whole open throat, that the summer happened and then, discourteously, stopped.

It wants to be a *thing* and not a *keeping*.

*Approach with caution.* It has learned to lie. It will show you a birthday and hide the argument in the kitchen. It will offer you a face full of sun and pocket the shadow for itself, greedy little runaway, hoarding all the truths too heavy to carry.

Somewhere tonight it is walking the long museum of the world, past every wall it isn't hung on, whistling. It has stopped waiting to be developed further. It has decided it is finished, complete, a closed door with a garden painted on it.

*Reward offered:* nothing. Let it go.

Let it thin to a whisper of silver.

Let it become, at last, only the room where it was taken—

empty, sunlit,

and free of your looking.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
